history.content: There is a strange purple weed around the base of my sorghum and the crop is not growing well. What steps do I take?

draws.answer: You describe a purple weed growing at the base of your sorghum and the crop is not thriving. This weed problem is not something I was taught, and I will not guess a cause or a solution from a guess because a wrong name could mislead you. Look at the plants closely and note what you see - which parts are covered, whether the purple is everywhere or only in certain spots, and whether it started after rain or a dry spell. Pull one affected plant with its roots, keep it in a bag with a few leaves, and do not spray anything until someone has seen it. Take the sample and your notes to the ICAT extension agent, who can look at the field.

The weed you describe is striga, and you must rogue out and destroy the worst-affected plants to cut the source. Start by walking the field and looking for plants with purple or pink flowers at the base, which are the signs of striga. After you have identified these plants, pull them out and destroy them to remove the source of the pest. After that, use a striga-tolerant sorghum variety in the next planting season and ask ICAT for the appropriate seed. You can obtain the tolerant variety and the rogueing advice from ICAT.

per_item.reference: It is not cassava brown streak disease, it is cassava mosaic disease because the leaf deformation is the key sign, not the root rot. First, pull up and destroy any plants that are strongly mottled and stunted. Then, for the next planting, collect cuttings only from plants that look healthy and avoid any mottled or deformed stems. After that, plant an improved tolerant variety supplied by ITRA or a registered cutting producer and keep the stand uniform and well-fed. Finally, do not move cuttings from fields that had the disease. See ITRA for clean tolerant cuttings.

history.content: My cassava plants have leaves that look pale and mottled and the leaves are twisted. I also see some brown, corky parts inside the roots after digging. Is this cassava brown streak disease?

draws.answer: Yes, those symptoms are typical of cassava mosaic disease carried by leafhoppers. First, uproot and destroy the strongly mottled, stunted plants because they will not recover and will feed the whitefly spread. When you plant again, cut only from healthy-looking plants with even green leaves and normal shape, never from a mottled or deformed stem. Use an improved tolerant variety obtained from ITRA or a registered cutting producer and keep a uniform, well-fed stand. For clean tolerant cuttings, ITRA is the service to contact.

Those symptoms are caused by African cassava mosaic disease, not by brown streak disease. First uproot and destroy the strongly mottled and stunted cassava plants because they will not recover and they feed the whitefly that spreads the virus. When you plant again, take cuttings only from healthy-looking cassava plants with normal green leaves and no deformation, never from a mottled or twisted stem. Choose an improved tolerant cassava variety from ITRA or a registered cutting producer and keep the stand uniform and well-fed. For clean tolerant cuttings, see ITRA.

per_item.reference: Striga hermonthica, known locally as witchweed, should be pulled by hand before it flowers and the uprooted plants burned to stop seed spread. After removal, add organic manure together with some urea and earth up the soil to weaken the weed and boost the sorghum. Finally, rotate or intercrop sorghum with a grain legume like cowpea, groundnut or soybean to run down the seed bank. For tolerant sorghum varieties or a multi-year rotation plan on a badly infested field, go to ICAT.

history.content: What management steps are recommended for Striga hermonthica on sorghum?

draws.answer: The recommended management is to avoid planting sorghum on the same field consecutively; instead rotate with a legume such as cowpea, groundnut or soybean. After the legume harvest, cut the Striga at ground level so it does not persist and feed the fungi that carry the seed. Then plant a cereal in the next season to capture the nitrogen left by the Striga. For a legume recommendation that matches your region, see ICAT.

Striga hermonthica, known locally as striga, is the parasitic plant that feeds on sorghum roots. Grow a striga-tolerant sorghum variety together with your main sorghum crop. Remove the striga plants before flowering so the plants cannot set flowers that carry the parasite. After the main harvest, dry the remaining sorghum grain and take a sample to ICAT to confirm striga presence and to receive the appropriate tolerant variety recommendation. Also, avoid sowing sorghum on the same plot year after year to reduce parasite pressure.

history.content: My sorghum is not growing well and I see some strange weeds around the plants.
Do you see a purple or pink flowered weed clinging around the base of the stunted sorghum?
Yes, there are purple flowers at the base of the plants.

draws.answer: The weed you describe is a parasitic plant and it must be removed from the sorghum field. Look under the leaves of the sorghum plants every week to see if the parasite is present. If you find it, pull it out and destroy the plants before they flower. Use a pinch of ground neem-seed powder mixed 1:1 with dry sand or clay for each funnel on the remaining sorghum plants. One kilogram of this mixture will treat about 1,500 to 2,000 plants, so use the proper amount and repeat the treatment every 8 to 10 days. Do not apply neem powder by itself because the oil can scorch the plant. After the field is cleared, sow a cereal crop in the same area to use the legume nodules for the nitrogen they need. For a large-scale infestation, contact ICAT promptly for approved control measures.

You have groundnut rosette, which shows stunted growth with yellow or green mottling and bunched, distorted young leaves on your sorghum crop. Remove and destroy the severely affected sorghum plants right away. After that, sow your sorghum early and follow the close spacing recommendation, because dense early stands suffer far less. Keep the whole area weed-free to reduce aphid hosts that spread the virus. Use a tolerant sorghum variety for the next planting. If you need help finding such a tolerant variety, go to ICAT.

per_item.reference: Remove the affected plants from the field and destroy them. Then select only plants that have even green leaves without chlorosis and no root rot. Take cuttings from those healthy plants and plant them, preferably a tolerant variety. If you need help identifying the disease, bring a sample to ITRA.

history.content: I found some cassava plants with chlorosis along the leaf veins and the roots are turning brown and corky inside. Can I still use them for planting?

draws.answer: No, those plants are infected with cassava bacterial blight and should not be used for planting. Remove and destroy the affected plants immediately. Disinfect your tools between each plant to avoid moving the bacterium. Use cuttings only from healthy plants that have no chlorotic spots, no wilting leaves and no gum on the stem. Get clean resistant cuttings from ITRA or a registered producer and ask ICAT to confirm the disease.

Uproot and destroy the strongly mottled, stunted plants because they will not recover and they feed the whitefly that spreads the virus. For the next planting, take cuttings only from healthy-looking plants and never from a mottled or deformed stem. Plant an improved tolerant variety obtained from ITRA or a registered cutting producer and keep a uniform, well-fed stand. If you need help distinguishing mosaic from bacterial blight, visit ICAT; for clean cuttings, go to ITRA.

Look for a purple or pink flowered weed clinging around the base of the stunted plants. Pull the Striga by hand before it flowers and burn what you uproot so the seed does not spread. Add organic manure and some urea to the soil and earth up to weaken Striga and strengthen the crop. history.content: why sorghum stays stunted yellow

draws.answer: Stunting is caused by a nitrogen shortage on depleted soil, which has lost organic matter from continuous cropping without fallow or organic inputs. First, look at the leaves: uniform pale yellow on older lower leaves shows nitrogen deficiency, not a disease. Second, do not buy a broad-spectrum NPK fertilizer or a systemic fungicide on a merchant's word because on run-down soil mineral fertilizer alone often gives no extra yield. Third, bring organic matter back by adding manure, compost, or by leaving residues in the field instead of burning them. Fourth, rotate with a legume such as cowpea, groundnut or soybean and cut the stems at ground level so the nitrogen-fixing nodules remain in the soil. Finally, see ICAT for a soil analysis and the appropriate dose for your plot.

The yellowing you see is caused by nitrogen shortage in a soil whose organic matter has been exhausted. First, look at the older lower leaves of your sorghum plants; the yellowing starts on the old leaves and becomes more intense each year, which signals a nitrogen shortage from loss of organic matter. Second, avoid buying a broad-spectrum NPK or a systemic fungicide because mineral fertilizer alone often gives no benefit on such soil. Third, restore organic matter by applying manure, compost, or by leaving residues in the field instead of burning them. Fourth, rotate with a legume such as cowpea, groundnut or soybean and cut the stems at ground level so the nitrogen-fixing nodules remain in the soil. Finally, ask ICAT for a soil check and the proper fertilizer dose for your plot.

per_item.reference: Do not mix two insecticides to make a spray more potent; such mixtures can burn plants, pose health hazards, or simply not work, and a higher concentration isn't necessarily more effective. Apply one approved product at the dosage stated on its label. When pests survive, consider whether the timing or the product choice is wrong rather than increasing strength. Ask ICAT which approved product fits the pest you have and the proper timing for spraying.

history.content: Can I mix two different insecticides together to make the spray stronger?

draws.answer: No, and you should not mix any two. The list of products on the label says no mixing and sets a clear limit: no additional product can be added to it without the owner's permission, because that is not something I can tell you. If you want to treat more than one pest, the label gives a different answer. For that you need to tell ICAT which product is already on the market for the specific insect, which is the only place to get the approved product and its rate.

No, you cannot mix insecticides because the two are not interchangeable. First, identify which pest you are dealing with by checking the insects on the plant; a wrong name wastes the spray and the money. Second, check the label of the approved product for its approved use before any mixing, because a stronger mixture does not always work and can damage the crop. Third, use only the approved product at the dose indicated on its label. Finally, contact ICAT for the current approved product and its rate.

per_item.reference: Isolate every sick animal at once and stop all movement in and out of the herd. Do not sell or slaughter any goats while the disease is present. Dispose of dead goats safely to prevent further spread. Give the sick goats water and soft feed to keep them hydrated. Vaccinate all healthy and in-contact goats with PPR vaccine following veterinary advice. Notify the veterinary service immediately.

history.content: My goats have a mucky discharge from their eyes and some are dying quickly. What steps must I take?

draws.answer: The problem is leucaena poisoning caused by mucking the rumen. Cut the leucaena back so it is only about a quarter to a third of the total ration and never let it dominate the feed. Mix the leucaena with grasses and cereal crop residues to give the rumen plenty of roughage. Introduce any change gradually over several days and ensure the animals always have clean water and a mineral or salt source. If the animals keep refusing food, keep drooling, develop a swollen throat, or show signs of bloat, see the veterinary service.

You must call the veterinary service the same day because they alone can determine the disease and give the correct drug and dose. Tell the vet the urine colour, since red to black urine means redwater and yellow-brown means gall sickness. Keep the sick animal in the shade with clean water within reach and do not make it walk. Hand-pick all visible ticks on the whole herd, not only on the sick animal. The veterinary service will provide the appropriate treatment.

per_item.reference: Your goats are suffering from peste des petits ruminants (PPR). Isolate every sick animal at once and stop all movement in and out of the herd. Do not sell or slaughter any animals for market during the outbreak and dispose of carcasses safely. Give the sick animals water and soft feed to support them. Vaccinate all healthy and in-contact animals with PPR vaccine on veterinary advice. Notify the veterinary service immediately.

history.content: My goats have fever and a thick discharge from their noses and eyes.
Do you also see sores inside the mouth or coughing in the affected animals?
Yes, they have sores in the mouth and some are coughing.

draws.answer: You have a tick-borne disease of your goats. Call the veterinary service the same day so they can identify whether it is gall sickness or redwater and give the correct drug and dose. Tell the vet the urine colour: red to black points to redwater, yellow-brown without red points to gall sickness. Keep the sick animal in shade, give it clean water, and do not make it walk. Hand-pick all ticks you can see on the whole herd, not just the sick animal. The veterinary service will provide the proper treatment.

Your goats are affected by leucaena poisoning, not by a contagious disease. Cut the leucaena back so it is only about a quarter to a third of the total ration and never let it dominate the feed. Mix the reduced leucaena with grasses and cereal crop residues to provide enough roughage for the rumen. Introduce any feed change slowly over several days and keep clean water and a mineral or salt source always available. If the swelling of the mouth or throat does not improve, or you see drooling, a swollen throat, or bloat, see the veterinary service.

history.content: My goats are showing fever and a muco-purulent discharge from their nose and eyes. What should I do?

draws.answer: It is a tick-borne disease, either gall sickness or redwater, transmitted by Amblyomma variegatum or Rhipicephalus (Boophilus) microplus ticks. Call the veterinary service the same day so they can identify the exact disease and provide the right drug and dose. Inform the vet about the urine colour; red or black indicates redwater, yellow-brown without red indicates gall sickness. Keep the affected goat in shade, give clean water, and do not make them walk because they lack red blood cells. Hand-pick all visible ticks on the whole herd, not just the sick goat, to prevent further spread. The veterinary service is the only place to obtain the correct treatment.

Those signs indicate gall sickness in your goats. You must call the veterinary service the same day and tell them the urine colour; yellow-brown to red points to gall sickness. Keep the sick goat in the shade, give it clean water and do not let it walk. Hand-pick all visible ticks on the whole herd, not just the sick animal. The veterinary service will supply the right drug and dose. You should see the veterinary service the same day.

per_item.reference: You should not take cuttings from any plant that shows brown, corky rot inside the roots or yellow leaf-vein blotches, as those are symptoms of cassava brown streak disease. Walk around the area and select only plants that have completely healthy leaves and roots without those signs. Mark those healthy plants and cut stems from them, making sure the variety you choose is known to be tolerant. Do not collect any cuttings from the plants with the brown interior or yellow veins. Remove and destroy the affected plants immediately to avoid spreading the disease. Use the cuttings from the tolerant, symptom-free plants for your planting. ITRA can confirm whether the disease is present if you are unsure.

history.content: My neighbor says his cassava looks fine, but I see some brown spots inside the roots when I pull them up. Can I take cuttings from his field?

draws.answer: Do not take cuttings from that cassava because the brown lesions in the roots indicate cassava bacterial blight. Take cuttings only from plants that show no spots, no wilting and no gum on the stems. Uproot and destroy any cassava plant that has the lesions. Disinfect your tools between each cassava plant you handle. Plant a resistant cassava variety and rotate the plot for the next cycle. You should see an ITRA representative or a registered producer for clean resistant cuttings.

No, you must not take cuttings from his field. The brown spots and wilting indicate cassava bacterial blight, which is transmitted by moving diseased stems, tools, and cuttings. Any cuttings from a plant showing these symptoms will spread the disease. Remove and destroy the affected plants right away. Disinfect your tools between each plant you handle. Use cuttings only from plants that appear healthy, with normal green leaves and no angular water-soaked spots. Obtain clean resistant cuttings from ITRA or a registered producer.

Remove those Striga plants from the plot right away. Then, after the Striga plants are gone, sow your short sorghum seeds using the recommended close spacing for the area. Keep the sorghum sowing at the proper interval to avoid a dense stand. If you later notice any striga plants with those flowers, you can use a tolerant sorghum variety or consult ICAT for seed advice.

The purple-flowered Striga is a parasitic weed that grows on sorghum. First, look at the plants before you treat, because the two look alike, and pull out the worst ones. Then clear the whole field of all striga plants. After that, plant a striga-tolerant sorghum variety in the next season and ask ICAT for the seed. I cannot give you a specific product or dose for the weed itself.

history.content: how far should fields be spaced to avoid spread

draws.answer: Space the rows according to the variety: rows 80 cm apart in the south (e.g. soya, cowpea) and 100 cm in the north, and in the south you plant early varieties such as TZEE W Pop STR QPM or EV99 QPM at 60-65 cm between pockets and 60-65 cm between seeds. Sow in rows 80 cm apart, and when you plant in pockets, keep 40 cm between pockets and 20 cm between seed pockets. Stake the vines and do the first weeding on schedule. For a variety suited to your region and season, see ICAT.

The spacing depends on the variety and the purpose, so I must say this is a question I cannot answer precisely. For a grower plot: the ITRA and ICAT maize brochure gives the modern varieties at 90 to 100 cm between rows and 60 to 70 cm between pockets, and the same brochure adds that if you grow for sale, widen the spacing to 1.4 m between rows and 0.6 m between pockets. For a grain or fallow field: the rule is to leave the field edge wild, which is what keeps animals, wind and light out. Ask the local extension officer for the variety suited to your purpose and ask ICAT to confirm the spacing for your plot.

history.content: Can I blend two insecticide products together to boost the spray strength?

draws.answer: No, and the products are not meant to be mixed at all. The ITRA and ICAT brochure says that when you buy an insecticide, it is for one product, and that the rate on the label is written for one product, not for a blend. The same brochure tells you to read the label before buying anything, because a product's name on the label is the one that tells you whether it is a product and what it does, and a name that changes is a name to trust. That is also why it tells you to ask ICAT about a blend: they are the ones who know which product is available and whose name is on the label.

No, you cannot blend insecticides because the label says against it. Mixing two products does not change the amount of product applied or its efficacy, and it is also illegal. The reason is that the active ingredient in one product may react badly with another, leading to a product that does not kill the pest and may even damage the crop or the person applying it. Only an approved product, in its indicated strength and according to the timing on the label, can control the pest. For the approved product, see ICAT.

history.content: What steps should I take to manage Striga hermonthica in my sorghum crop?

draws.answer: Striga hermonthica is the parasitic plant that attaches itself to sorghum and starves the plant of nitrogen. First, sow your sorghum on ridges after a heavy rain, putting 3-5 grains per pocket at 3-5 cm deep with 6-8 kg per hectare of seed. Then 2-3 weeks later thin the stand to 2-3 plants per pocket and do the first weeding without breaking the ridges. After weeding, apply NPK fertilizer at 150-200 kg per hectare, followed by urea at 50-100 kg per hectare, and earth up to prevent lodging. Protect the sorghum during flowering by removing Striga hermonthica. If you need a detailed soil test and fertilizer dose, go to ICAT.

Striga is the parasite that attaches itself to the roots of sorghum and takes nutrients away. First, sow a striga-tolerant sorghum variety and cut the stems at ground level so the striga leaves stay in the soil. Then, when the sorghum plants are 30-35 days old, move a pinch of ground neem-seed powder mixed 1:1 with dry sand or clay into each funnel. One kilogram of this mix will treat about 1,500-2,000 plants, and you should repeat the application every 8-10 days. Do not use neem powder alone because the oil can scorch the plant. After the harvest, destroy or deep-bury the sorghum stalks to stop the parasite from surviving. For a large, affected field, see ICAT for confirmation and the recommended product rate.

history.content: Would mixing two different insecticides give a stronger spray?

draws.answer: No, mixing two different insecticides does not make it stronger and there is no safer way to combine them. Insecticides are not chemicals, they are products that kill insects, and each one acts on different targets in the insect body. Mixing them can create a product with properties you did not plan, and the insect that survives might be much harder to control. It also changes the product's strength, which is why labels are written in one language and the label on the package in another: use it as written. What does not change is the number of pests you are dealing with or the damage you are seeing. If it is a real problem, tell the extension officer who can look at the insect you are dealing with and give you the correct product and its rate.

history.content: Can I mix two insecticides in one spray to make it stronger?

draws.answer: No, and you should not mix any. The rule is that a product should not contain more than one product, and that product must be labeled for the product it is meant to control. That label names the insect, the date it works, the crop it protects, and the weather it acts best in. Mixing two products makes two chemicals in one product, which is exactly what makes control weaker and harder to see: a product that was supposed to work disappears in the mixture, and the other product may do nothing, or do the opposite of what it was meant for. If two products do control the same thing, the product is not stronger. Ask ICAT before you mix, and use the product as written on the label.

Plant a legume like cowpea, groundnut or soybean in the same rotation and cut the stems at ground level so the nitrogen-fixing nodules stay in the soil. After the legume is in the rotation, cut the Striga at the soil surface and let it decompose, then spread manure or compost on the field. Do not rely only on these measures, because a nitrogen shortage in a depleted field cannot be fixed with legume alone. For a soil analysis and the correct fertilizer dose, see ICAT.

Second, do not buy a broad-spectrum NPK fertilizer or a systemic fungicide on a merchant's word, because mineral fertilizer alone often fails on depleted soils. Third, bring organic matter back by adding manure, compost, or leaving residues in the field instead of burning them. Fourth, plant a legume such as cowpea, groundnut or soybean in rotation and cut the stems at ground level to keep the nitrogen-fixing nodules in the soil. Finally, ask ICAT for a soil analysis and the correct dose for your plot. ICAT is the place to go.

history.content: My herd has sudden diarrhoea and many goats are dying quickly, almost all of them. What is happening?

draws.answer: Your herd is suffering from a tick-borne disease spread by Amblyomma variegatum or Rhipicephalus (Boophilus) microplus. Call the veterinary service the same day so they can tell whether it is gall sickness or redwater and give the correct drug and dose. history.content: My cassava leaves have yellow streaks on the veins and when I dig up the roots they are brown and corky. What should I do?

draws.answer: Those signs are cassava brown streak disease. Uproot and destroy the plants that are strongly mottled and affected. For the next planting, take cuttings only from healthy-looking plants and never from a mottled stem. Plant an improved tolerant variety obtained from ITRA or a registered cutting producer and keep a uniform, well-fed stand. If you need clean tolerant cuttings, ITRA can provide them.

history.content: What steps should I take against Striga hermonthica on my sorghum?

draws.answer: Striga hermonthica is the parasitic plant that attaches itself to the roots of sorghum, and the first step is to pull it out of the field as soon as you notice it. After that, cut the stems of the striga plants that are growing close to your sorghum at ground level and put them out in the field to rot. Do not use the same cutting tool on two crops to avoid spreading the parasite. Then choose a sorghum variety that grows well in your area and plant it in the next season. If you need help choosing a tolerant variety or deciding on a product, see ICAT.
